source: Hales et al. (2015) A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture
finding: Human referees of the 1998 Kepler proof could not check every step of the computer parts. A team re-proved it in HOL Light plus Isabelle, so a small kernel checked all steps.
numbers: Referees published without complete certification (Lagarias report). Main statement re-checks in about 5 hours on a 2 GHz CPU from proof scripts. Some subclaims take over a day each; the hardest about 5000 CPU hours.
quote: The kernel of HOL Light is remarkably small, amounting to just a few hundred lines of code.
limits: Project took over a decade. The formal proof matches a specific statement; statement fidelity is still human-checked.
agent_relevance: S8 should treat the kernel verdict as the only trusted verifier. Heavy checks can cost a lot of compute, so budget them.

source: Hales et al. (2015) A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture (kernel trust)
finding: Trust comes from the LCF design: only a few hundred lines of kernel code can make a theorem, and the kernel itself was formally verified.
numbers: HOL Light kernel: a few hundred lines of OCaml. Formal verification of its correctness cited (Harrison).
quote: It is generally held by experts that it is extremely unlikely for the HOL Light proof assistant to create a 'false' theorem.
limits: Trust is in the logic and kernel, not in tactics or search code. A wrongly stated theorem still passes.
agent_relevance: Design rule: the model may propose anything; only the kernel accepts. This is the cleanest external verifier an agent can have (supports G2, G3).

source: mathlib Community (2020) The Lean mathematical library
finding: Describes mathlib, a community library in Lean 3 where all proofs are kernel-checked. It became the main corpus for later neural provers.
numbers: Grew from 15k to 140k lines of code (excluding blanks and comments); 73 contributors, 11 maintainers. PACT paper (2021) cites 46,000+ lemmas, 21,000+ definitions.
limits: Lean 3 library, later ported to Lean 4. Counts are 2020-21 snapshots.
agent_relevance: Mathlib is training data for LLM provers, so contamination risk when scoring an agent.

source: Polu and Sutskever (2020) Generative language modeling for automated theorem proving
finding: GPT-f: a transformer proposes proof steps for Metamath, and best-first search with kernel checking assembles proofs. First strong language-model result in a proof assistant.
numbers: Closes 56.22% of the held-out set.mm test set (1k proofs) versus 21.16% for the earlier MetaGen-IL. Training from about 38k set.mm proofs.
limits: Metamath has no tactics; proof depth 10 to 20 steps versus 1 to 3 in Coq, HOL Light or Lean. Not comparable across systems.
agent_relevance: Pattern for our agent: model proposes, search plus kernel disposes.

source: Polu and Sutskever (2020) Generative language modeling for automated theorem proving (value function, self-improvement)
finding: Training a value function on statements the prover itself generated improved the prover. This suggests a loop: keep training on kernel-verified proofs the prover found.
numbers: Model size correlated positively with pass rate. Ablation of synthetic data augmentation helped (Table 10, 160M and 700M models).
limits: Shown for Metamath only.
agent_relevance: Kernel-checked output is a clean reward signal. A scaffold without training can still use it for selection (G5).

source: Polu and Sutskever (2020) Generative language modeling for automated theorem proving (real contributions)
finding: GPT-f found 23 shorter proofs of existing theorems that the Metamath community accepted into set.mm. Axiom use was checked.
numbers: 23 proofs accepted into the main library.
limits: Shortening is a narrow task.
agent_relevance: Shows verified novelty: a kernel confirms a new output is correct without a human reading it.

source: Han et al. (2021) Proof Artifact Co-Training for theorem proving with language models
finding: PACT trains on auxiliary tasks extracted from proof terms (masked subterms, next lemma, proof terms) alongside tactic prediction. This reduced overfitting and raised the pass rate on held-out mathlib theorems.
numbers: Held-out mathlib pass rate 32% to 48% (best row WebMath > mix1 > tactic 48.4%; tactic-only rows 39.8 to 44.0% by pre-training). Baselines: refl 9.9%, tidy-bfs 32.2%. Out-of-distribution theorems: 37%.
limits: Single split of mathlib; later mathlib versions may overlap web pre-training. Mix choice moved results by a few points.
agent_relevance: Extra views of verified data help. For a no-training scaffold, the analog is reusing checker output as context.

source: Zheng, Han and Polu (2021) miniF2F: a cross-system benchmark for formal Olympiad-level mathematics
finding: Introduces miniF2F: 488 problems (244 valid, 244 test) from AMC, AIME, IMO and course material, formalized for Metamath, Lean, partly Isabelle and HOL Light.
numbers: Lean tidy baseline 12/244 valid, 13/244 test. Lean GPT-f imax=1: 29/244 test; imax 4 to 128: 43-44/244 test (about 18%) and 41/244 valid. Metamath GPT-f Pass@1 1.3%, Pass@8 1.6% on test.
limits: Statements formalized by hand. Small benchmark: one problem is 0.4 points.
agent_relevance: Common yardstick. Note the plateau after imax=4: more sampling gave no gain for that model.

source: Zheng, Han and Polu (2021) miniF2F: a cross-system benchmark for formal Olympiad-level mathematics (cross-system gap)
finding: Same problem set shows the system gap: Metamath has no tactics so proofs are long and the model scores near zero; Lean tactics give short proofs.
numbers: Metamath GPT-f 1.3% Pass@1 on miniF2F-test versus 56.22% on its own library test.
limits: Different tools trained on different data; distribution shift from library to competition problems.
agent_relevance: Library performance overstates competition performance. Do not read a headline number across benchmarks.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Thor: wielding hammers to integrate language models and automated theorem provers
finding: Thor lets the language model decide when to call Sledgehammer (Isabelle's hammer: premise selection, external provers, proof reconstruction inside the kernel). Combining beats either alone.
numbers: PISA: success 39.0% to 57.0%; solves 8.2% of problems neither the LM nor Sledgehammer solves. Sledgehammer alone 25.7%. MiniF2F: 29.6% to 29.9%.
limits: LM premise selection is weak: only 1.9% of premise-bearing LM steps advanced the proof, versus 28.2% of steps with no premises.
agent_relevance: Hybrid wins: learned proposer for structure, symbolic tool for gaps. The tool's verdict stays external.

source: Bohme and Nipkow (2010) Sledgehammer: judgement day
finding: Not opened. From memory: Sledgehammer sends a goal plus selected facts to external provers, then rebuilds the proof with Isabelle's own methods, so the kernel never trusts the outside prover.
numbers: Recalled, unverified: evaluation on about 1240 goals from 7 theories, roughly half solved automatically. Verify before use.
limits: Not opened this session; numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as S8: outside tool proposes, trusted checker reconstructs.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur: whole-proof generation and repair with large language models
finding: Fine-tuned LLMs write a whole Isabelle proof at once, then a second model repairs it using the proof assistant's error message. Combining with Thor adds more.
numbers: On 6336 theorems: 8b generate 34.8% (16 samples), 40.7% (64); with theory-file context 47.5%; 62b with context 47.9% (only +0.4 over 8b). Baldur 8b + Thor 65.7% versus Thor alone 58.0%. Sledgehammer 25.6%, search-based LM 39.0%. Repair added about 1.5 points.
limits: Isabelle only. Size mattered little once context was given.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: revise from real checker output. File context mattered more than model size.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove
finding: An LLM drafts an informal proof, turns it into a formal sketch with gaps, then Sledgehammer plus heuristics fill the gaps and Isabelle checks. Informal proofs add measurable value.
numbers: MiniF2F: success 20.9% to 39.3% with human informal proofs; 38.9% with LLM-written ones (abstract and Table 1, test split). Ablations on human-informal setup: no in-line comments -4.9, no informal proofs -3.7, no automated provers -9.8 points.
limits: Exact column assignment of baseline rows in the table text was unclear, so only headline and ablation values are recorded.
agent_relevance: Plan in language, formalize the skeleton, let a mechanical tool close gaps, verify. The tool mattered more than the informal writer.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (scale of informal writer)
finding: A larger informal-proof writer did not help the final proof rate.
numbers: Minerva informal proofs: 8B 36.5% (-2.8), 62B 34.0% (-5.3), 540B 30.3% (-9.0) on test.
limits: Differences may reflect style of drafts, not ability.
agent_relevance: Bigger generator is not a better plan for the formalizer.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo: theorem proving with retrieval-augmented language models
finding: ReProver adds premise retrieval to a tactic-generating model for Lean. It beats no retrieval and zero-shot GPT-4, especially when premises are new.
numbers: Pass@1 random split: ReProver 51.2%, without retrieval 47.6%, GPT-4 29.0%, tidy 23.8%. Novel-premises split: 26.3, 23.2, 7.4, 5.3. MiniF2F 26.5%, ProofNet 13.8%. Training 120 GPU hours (5 days, one GPU).
limits: Random split inflates scores because proofs share premises; novel-premises split is the honest test.
agent_relevance: Evaluate on novel-premise splits. Retrieval of the right fact is a bottleneck a tool can address.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo: theorem proving with retrieval-augmented language models (harness error)
finding: Earlier tooling marked correct ground-truth proofs as wrong; LeanDojo fixed this.
numbers: Ground-truth proofs misjudged as incorrect fell from 21.1% to 1.4%.
limits: The harness around the kernel can create false failures.
agent_relevance: Check the checker harness. A false reject is a measurement error, not a reasoning error.

source: Lample et al. (2022) HyperTree Proof Search for neural theorem proving
finding: HTPS uses AND-OR hypertree search with online training on found proofs. Strong gains on Metamath and Lean miniF2F.
numbers: Metamath held-out 65.4% supervised (GPT-f 56.5%); with online training 82.6% cumulative. MiniF2F-valid 58.6% cumulative; miniF2F-test 41% pass@64 versus 36.6% GPT-f; without synthetic co-training task 54.9% valid and 38.5% test.
limits: Cumulative rates count any success during training and the online step sees the unproved targets. Not single-shot.
agent_relevance: Cumulative numbers blur train and test. Treat carefully.

source: Song et al. (2024) Lean Copilot
finding: A human-in-the-loop Lean tool that calls LLM suggestions and search. It cuts how many tactics a human types.
numbers: Automates 74.2% of proof steps on average versus 40.1% for AESOP (85% better). Manual tactics needed 2.08 versus 3.86 for AESOP.
limits: Small test on selected theorems.
agent_relevance: Human plus tool works: model fills steps, kernel keeps trust.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5
finding: Whole-proof generation with reinforcement learning from proof-assistant feedback, plus tree search for exploration.
numbers: MiniF2F-test 60.2% single pass (V1: 50.0%); 63.5% with tree search; 51.6% at 128 samples. ProofNet valid 21.6%, test 23.7%; with tree search 25.4% valid, 25.3% test.
limits: Pass rates depend on sampling budget. Lean 4 only.
agent_relevance: Verifier feedback as reward works; always state budget.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2
finding: Recursive subgoal decomposition: a general LLM splits the problem, a 7B prover solves each piece, and the combined traces seed reinforcement learning.
numbers: MiniF2F-test 88.9% (671B); 47 of 658 PutnamBench problems solved.
limits: About 7% of PutnamBench solved, so hard undergraduate problems remain. High sampling budgets.
agent_relevance: Decomposition into separately verifiable lemmas scales; fits a scaffold that splits then checks each part.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2
finding: Scaffolded data synthesis, verifier-guided self-correction from compiler feedback, and model averaging. Small models match larger ones.
numbers: 32B: 88.1% pass@32 on MiniF2F, 90.4% with self-correction. 8B: 84.6% pass@32. PutnamBench: 86/657 (as cited by Seed-Prover).
limits: MiniF2F nearly saturated; possible training-distribution overlap.
agent_relevance: Self-correction from compiler output added 2.3 points: G2 revise from real output holds in formal domains.

source: ByteDance Seed (2025) Seed-Prover
finding: Lemma-style whole-proof model refining proofs from Lean feedback, proved lemmas and self-summaries, with three test-time strategies. Used at IMO 2025.
numbers: 78.1% of formalized past IMO problems; saturates MiniF2F; PutnamBench 331/657 (medium setting); IMO 2025: 5 of 6 fully proved.
limits: Heavy test-time compute. Geometry needed a separate engine (Seed-Geometry).
agent_relevance: Storing proved lemmas and iterating on checker feedback gives large gains: memory plus verify loop.

source: Tsoukalas et al. (2024) PutnamBench
finding: Hard benchmark of 1692 formalizations of 640 Putnam problems in Lean 4 and Isabelle (some Coq). At release almost nothing was solved.
numbers: Lean 4 (640): GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, ReProver 0. Isabelle (640): DSP 4, Sledgehammer 3. Coq (412): GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, Tactician 0, CoqHammer 0.
limits: 2024 snapshot; Seed-Prover reports 331/657 a year later.
agent_relevance: Benchmark half-life is short; do not trust old difficulty claims.

source: Synthesis: where checking helps (Baldur, Thor, Goedel)
finding: Kernel or compiler feedback gave gains in every system tested; the largest came from combining a language proposer with a symbolic tool.
numbers: Baldur +7.7 over Thor alone (65.7 vs 58.0); Thor 39.0 to 57.0 over LM alone; Goedel +2.3 from self-correction.
limits: Derived from lines above; not a new source.
agent_relevance: Apply the checker, feed the real error back once, keep a symbolic fallback.

source: Synthesis: context beats scale
finding: Model size gave little once the right context was present.
numbers: Baldur 62b only +0.4 over 8b; DSP Minerva 36.5 to 30.3 as size grew; LeanDojo retrieval 51.2 vs 47.6.
limits: Derived from lines above.
agent_relevance: Spend effort on context and tools, not a bigger generator.

source: Synthesis: boundary conditions and inflation
finding: Library-test scores are inflated by shared premises; competition and undergraduate sets score far lower; benchmarks saturate within about a year.
numbers: Metamath 56.22% in-library vs 1.3% on miniF2F; ReProver 51.2% random vs 26.3% novel premises; PutnamBench near 0 in 2024.
limits: Derived.
agent_relevance: Test on held-out splits and report budget; assume leaderboard numbers are optimistic.
